title: Dearer than a son
hookLine: a line that sounds selfish until you see which self it means
carry: the atman is where love lives
tomorrow: Yajnavalkya and his two wives: he's leaving
last: ONE SELF FELL IN TWO: YOU ARE THE HALF.

lines: THE SELF IS DEARER THAN A SON.
cards: Three hundred sixty-five. One day at a time, that's a whole calendar year on this path. Now a question that sounds like a trap.
Ask a parent: who do you love more, your child or yourself? The answer may come before the question ends. My child.
Obviously. Yet the Brihadaranyaka says, flatly, the self is dearer than a son. It sounds selfish.
It sounds wrong. Stay with it, because the whole line turns on one small Sanskrit word.

teach.b: Here's the line in full. This self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else, because it is more inward. That's the small word: antaratara, more inner, closer in.
One way to read it: the text isn't measuring how much anyone loves. It's asking where love lives. When you love your child, where is that love felt?
Not in the child. In you, from the inside. The self here is the atman, the deep self, not your ego, your reputation, your wants.

teach.h: NOT THE EGO: THE ONE AT THE CENTER.
teach.b: Two days ago we met aham asmi, I am, before any name, and Vedanta readers hear that self here: the one at the center, the place every love is felt from. Then the text adds a warning.
If someone calls anything else most dear, and another person tells them, you'll lose what you love, it may well come true. A son can be lost. Wealth can be lost.

teach.h: WHAT YOU HOLD DEAR CAN BE LOST.
teach.b: So, the text says, hold the self alone as dear, and what you hold dear won't perish. The schools of Vedanta read this self in different ways.
Advaita hears the one self that is also the self of your son, so loving it leaves nobody out. Devotional schools hear the soul, whose own inner self is God.

teach.h: LOVE IS LIT FROM THE INSIDE.
teach.b: Neither hears permission to love a child less. A conversation later in this book makes the same point about a husband and a wife.

teach.h: THE ATMAN IS WHERE LOVE LIVES.
teach.b: That's the teaching: the atman, not the ego, is where every love is felt, and the one dear thing that won't perish. So when a Hindu elder says the self comes first, on this reading she isn't ranking her children.
She's naming where her love for them lives.

how: Teachers of Vedanta use this passage to explain that the atman, not the ego, is the source of all love; it is read alongside Yajnavalkya's teaching to Maitreyi later in the same Upanishad.

o: dear, beloved, the one held closest

games.q: what's inside the line — tap the pairs.
p: not the ego: the one at the center

s: this line tells parents to love their children less
it asks where love lives, not how much. no school reads it as permission to love a child less.
the reason the text gives is that the self is more inward
antaratara: more inner. every love is felt from there.
"self" here means your ego and its wants
it means the self at the center, the I am before any name.

games.q: someone calls a thing other than the self most dear, and a friend warns them: you'll lose what you love. what does the text say?
o: the friend is wrong; love protects it.
it depends on how much they love it.
games.why: it may well come true: sons and wealth can be lost. so the text says to hold the self as dear, and what you hold dear won't perish.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love without effort: a child, a parent, a friend, a pet, and let the feeling come. Then, gently, notice where you're feeling it from: not where they are, but here, in you.
Rest in that warm center, and notice it was there before they came to mind, and is still there now.

wordCard.voice: Priya, dear, beloved. Dearer than wealth, dearer than all else, the Brihadaranyaka says, because it is more inward.

orig.note: Sanskrit priya: dear, beloved. the line says the self is preyas, dearer, than a son.
